prompt: The link between your two data centers drops. Should each side keep accepting writes or refuse them until the link is back?
tells: link between your two data centers drops
keep accepting writes or refuse them
why: During a partition you choose availability (accept, reconcile later) or consistency (refuse).
trap: There's no option that keeps both while the link is down.

prompt: A bank's balance service rejects requests during a network split, while the same company's "likes" counter keeps working and fixes counts later.
tells: rejects requests during a network split
keeps working and fixes counts later
why: Different data, different CAP choice: consistency for money, availability for likes.
trap: Same company, same network; the choice is per use case.

prompt: A shopping cart must always accept items even if replicas can't talk to each other; merging duplicate items later is acceptable.
tells: replicas can't talk to each other
why: An AP choice: stay available during partitions and reconcile afterwards (as Dynamo did).
trap: This is a design choice, not a bug to fix.

prompt: A database leader gets cut off from the majority of its replicas. It stops accepting writes, and clients see errors until a new leader is elected.
why: A CP system gives up availability on the minority side to avoid conflicting writes.
trap: The errors are the cost of consistency, by design.

prompt: During a network split, DNS resolvers keep answering with cached records that may be outdated rather than failing lookups.
tells: cached records that may be outdated
why: DNS chooses availability over consistency under partition: stale answers beat no answers.
trap: Caching is the mechanism; the choice under partition is the principle.

prompt: An event site lets both regions sell seats while their link is down, then discovers 40 seats were sold twice.
why: Choosing availability during a partition means accepting conflicting writes; for unique seats, consistency was the right call.
trap: This isn't a bug in the code; it's the trade-off they picked.

prompt: A store with 5 replicas requires 3 to acknowledge each write. When 3 replicas are on the far side of a split, the 2-replica side rejects writes.
tells: on the far side of a split
why: Majority quorums keep consistency by giving up availability on the minority side of a partition.
trap: Waiting for 3 acks also affects tail latency, but rejection during a split is CAP.

prompt: A notes app lets you edit on a plane with no connection and merges changes when you land, sometimes showing both versions.
tells: edit on a plane with no connection
why: Offline is the extreme partition; the app picks availability and reconciles later.
trap: Merge logic is the cost of that choice, not a separate principle.
